title: Pylon: an AWS platform for AI agents
intro: Pylon is an AWS runtime for internal AI agents, built in Terraform and mapped to each point of Swisscom's AI Platform Engineer job post. The code passes its tests offline; live tests are in progress.

verdict.headline: Pylon: an AWS runtime for internal AI agents
lede: I built Pylon to answer Swisscom's AI Platform Engineer job post, one point at a time. It runs an AI agent on Fargate behind Entra sign-in, writes an audit record for every query, alarms on its SLOs and scales itself to zero at a EUR 30 monthly cap.
The code and its tests pass offline. Nothing is verified live in AWS yet: live tests are in progress. Each row below has a badge that says which state it's in.
verdict.adoptHeading: What you can adopt on day one
adopt: Nine Terraform modules (network, KMS, edge, agent service, tools, audit, observability, chaos, FinOps), composed into dev, staging and prod roots, each with its own state.
A front door with no load balancer and no NAT gateway: CloudFront and WAF, an HTTP API that checks the Entra token, then a VPC Link to the agent on Fargate.
A model gateway to Bedrock with a second model as fallback, and a canned answer when both fail.
One audit record per query in an S3 Object Lock bucket, queryable in Athena.
Six alarms on five SLIs, with the error-budget math written out in the SLO document.
A per-user daily token quota, a daily cost report by team, and a budget kill switch that scales the agent to zero.
Five runbooks and a STRIDE threat model over five trust boundaries.
adapt: Identity: point the JWT authorizer at your Entra tenant, audience and roles claim. Mine is a free test tenant.
Network: dev runs in one availability zone on public subnets. The prod setting (private subnets, two zones, VPC endpoints) exists in code and has never been applied.
Deploys: my AWS Organization blocks GitHub OIDC, so I deploy from my terminal (D-44). The OIDC roles are written and tested behind one flag. Turn it on if your organization allows it.
Region and models: I picked eu-north-1 because of Bedrock availability (D-19). Check which models your account can call.
SLO targets: these are my starting values for a dev demo, not contracted levels.
Standards: I don't know Swisscom's security, compliance or network rules. Every guess I made is in the assumptions file.

decisions.heading: Decisions and runbooks
decisions.intro: Every choice has an entry in the decision log: what, why, the alternatives I rejected, and which point of the job post it answers. The eight below shape this page.

items.title: Runtime: ECS Fargate agent plus Lambda tools
Model access: AWS Bedrock behind a thin gateway
Front door: CloudFront and WAF, then HTTP API, VPC link, Cloud Map, Fargate. No ALB.
Hard dev budget cap: EUR 30 per month
SLO targets and multi-window burn-rate alarms (dev demo)
Deploys are manual: the Organization SCP blocks GitHub OIDC

decisions.runbooksIntro: Each runbook ends with the date it was last run in dev. None has run yet.

gaps.heading: What this project cannot show
gaps.intro: These are the limits of a solo project that matter for this role.
items: Kubernetes. I chose ECS Fargate over EKS on cost (D-04). Pylon has no Kubernetes in it.
High availability. Dev runs in a single availability zone by design (D-14). The two-zone prod setting is code only.
On-call history. Pylon has never served real users, so there's no on-call record to show.
Pairing with security teams. I wrote the threat model alone. No security team has reviewed it.
Swisscom's own standards. I don't know them. Every Swisscom-specific guess is in the assumptions file.
Live evidence. Nothing is verified in AWS yet. Live tests are in progress, and a badge changes only when its evidence is linked.
